claims.text: Ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering can produce a non-equilibrium Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloy.
The ball-milled initial alloy is metastable.
The initial alloy contains a mixture of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
A targeted small Ti addition during ball milling and SPS triggers in situ formation of fine, dispersed Ti-rich oxides.
The Ti-rich oxide phases form at grain boundaries and intermetallic interfaces.
Targeted Ti addition promotes formation of a TiO2-rich surface film.
A Ti-rich surface film provides passivation in ball-milled and SPS-consolidated Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
The Ti-rich oxides transform the metastable microstructure into a stabilized, refined intermetallic composite.
Ti-rich oxides impede the diffusion of corrosive ions.
Ti-rich oxides impede oxygen diffusion at high temperature.
The Ti-added material will have a lower corrosion current density than an otherwise identically processed Ti-free control.
The Ti-added material will exhibit slower high-temperature oxidation kinetics and reduced oxidation weight gain relative to the Ti-free control.
At 50 MPa, an SPS temperature around 1050 °C can yield nearly full density with minimal porosity.
Rapid SPS densification and short high-temperature exposure limit grain growth.
A dwell time of approximately 3 minutes is suitable for the proposed SPS treatment.
The processed alloy can be maintained at a density below 6 g/cm3 under the proposed SPS conditions.
Comparable alloys processed conventionally or without Ti have higher corrosion rates because they form less effective passive films.
The hypothesis is limited to systems in which intermetallic formation and oxide passivation dominate corrosion and oxidation behavior.

contradictions.description: The mediator is described as dispersed oxide phases at internal grain boundaries and intermetallic interfaces, whereas the mechanism relies on a surface TiO2-rich passive film; the relationship between these internal oxides and the external film is not specified.
